This portrait catches the desperation of destitution. One also sees the powerlessness of the poor girl in her eyes. The girl does not look with jealousy, resentment or any sense of entitlement at all. She pleads only for pity. There is no sense of obligation implied by the painting, I feel. To me, the girl has a consciousness of an equivalent plight in those to whom she begs. Because it is a painting, one is able to gaze far longer that would be usual at such a sight. One does not feel lessened, at the time, by grudgingly providing a coin.

Perhaps the sense of the depth of this plight comes from the genuineness, one feels the sincerity. One trusts the painting. It does not inspire doubt or any skepticism, only empathy. The girl seeks relief from long standing poverty, which she struggles to bear.

To the right of the painting, in the movement of the brush, one can almost see an angelic wing, or even a figure kneeling in prayer. Perhaps the artist was haunted by a site he once saw.
